clinicalPearls: The most common inherited form of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, caused by loss-of-function variants in AVPR2 encoding the renal V2 vasopressin receptor.
X-linked recessive: affected boys usually present in early infancy with polyuria, polydipsia, poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive, unexplained fevers and episodes of hypernatraemic dehydration.
The collecting duct cannot respond to vasopressin, so urine remains inappropriately dilute despite a raised plasma osmolality.
Characteristically there is no urinary concentrating response to desmopressin, distinguishing it from central (cranial) diabetes insipidus.
Heterozygous female carriers may show variable concentrating defects owing to skewed X-inactivation, ranging from asymptomatic to overtly polyuric.
Recurrent hypernatraemic episodes in infancy risk neurological injury and developmental delay if not promptly recognised and managed.
Chronic high urine flow can produce a dilated urinary tract, megacystis and hydronephrosis.
Management centres on unrestricted access to water and measures that lower urine volume by reducing solute load; the condition contrasts with the autosomal AQP2 (aquaporin-2) forms.
reference.pathophysiology: AVPR2 on Xq28 encodes the arginine vasopressin receptor 2 (the V2 receptor), a G-protein-coupled receptor on the basolateral membrane of principal cells in the renal collecting duct. Vasopressin binding normally activates Gs-adenylate cyclase-cyclic AMP signalling, which drives insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane and permits water reabsorption. Loss-of-function variants, most often causing receptor misfolding with retention in the endoplasmic reticulum, abolish this signalling so that circulating vasopressin can no longer concentrate the urine. Because the gene is X-linked, hemizygous males are affected while heterozygous females show variable phenotypes governed by X-inactivation. Variants in the downstream water-channel gene AQP2 (aquaporin-2) cause the rarer autosomal recessive and dominant forms, which are clinically similar but differ in inheritance.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive and dominant nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from AQP2 (aquaporin-2) variants
Central (cranial) diabetes insipidus / arginine vasopressin deficiency
Acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, obstructive uropathy)
Osmotic diuresis, for example in poorly controlled diabetes mellitus
Bartter syndrome and other salt-wasting tubulopathies presenting with infantile polyuria
Fanconi syndrome and other generalised tubular concentrating defects
additionalInvestigations: Paired plasma and urine osmolality alongside plasma sodium
Water deprivation test with a desmopressin challenge (no urinary concentration after desmopressin in nephrogenic disease)
Copeptin measurement as a surrogate for vasopressin secretion
AVPR2 molecular genetic testing, with AQP2 analysis if AVPR2 is negative
Renal tract ultrasound for hydronephrosis and bladder dilatation
Review for acquired causes, including drug history, calcium and potassium
redFlags: Hypernatraemic dehydration with seizures or reduced consciousness in an infant
Failure to thrive with recurrent unexplained fevers
Progressive hydronephrosis or a chronically distended bladder
Over-rapid correction of hypernatraemia risking cerebral oedema
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, reliable access to water and volume-reducing measures, most affected individuals grow and develop normally; the principal threats are neurodevelopmental sequelae from repeated hypernatraemic episodes and urinary tract dilatation from chronic polyuria.
pitfalls: Mistaking recurrent infantile fevers and irritability for sepsis rather than hypernatraemic dehydration
Expecting a desmopressin response, which does not occur and distinguishes the condition from central diabetes insipidus
Attributing the polyuria simply to behavioural excessive drinking
